newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland detail one-tonne bomb find.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland detail one-tonne bomb find.

text.p: Northern Ireland police said on Saturday a bomb believed planted after Britain spelled out tough demands for Irish nationalist entry into peace talks contained more than a tonne of explosive, primed and ready for use.

The bomb, concealed under hay bales on a tractor trailer, was found on Friday in a field close to a British army barracks near the border town of Armagh. No group has claimed responsibility for assembling or planting it.

The discovery has raised fears of a new offensive by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) to protest against the latest British government statement setting out how the guerrilas' political wing, Sinn Fein, could join other political parties at Northern Ireland peace talks under way in Belfast.

British Prime Minister John Major told parliament on Thursday the IRA, which wants to end British rule and see the province reunified with the Irish republic, would have to call a credible and verifiable ceasefire before Sinn Fein could be admitted to the five-month-old negotiations.

He rejected Sinn Fein demands that it be granted automatic and immediate inclusion in the talks if the IRA called a new truce and said the guerrillas would have to prove the ceasefire was not a tactical ploy by renouncing violence for good.

Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's chief negotiator, said on Friday night the IRA would reject Major's terms if he approached them to restore the 17-month truce the guerrillas ended in February with bomb attacks in London.
Since then the guerrillas have staged further bomb attacks on the British mainland, in Germany and in Northern Ireland itself.

The IRA's ideological foes, pro-British Protestant Unionist parties, have broadly welcomed Major's refusal to accept Sinn Fein's demands, which were conveyed to the London government by Northern Irish peace broker John Hume, head of the moderate Irish nationalist SDLP group.
But Ian Paisley, head of the most right-wing Unionist party, told his annual conference that Major's statement was a betrayal which masked an intention to get Sinn Fein to the talks at any cost.

Paisley said Major had made no mention in his statement of the controversial issue of disarming rival pro-Irish and pro-British guerrillas and said he wanted it reinstated as a precondition for their representation at the peace talks.

Britain in February dropped its insistence that the IRA disarm before Sinn Fein could come to the negotiating table. It now says it will be satisfied if the guerrillas disarm in stages as the peace talks, chaired by former U.S. Senator George Mitchell, progress.

Paisley said Major's decision to abandon arms surrender as a condition of Sinn Fein's entry to the talks was a sell-out to the Irish Republic government, Britain's partner in the search for a settlement to the 27-year conflict which has so far killed 3,200 people.
"I believe John Major wanted to pretend to be a strong man so that behind backs he could sell out to the IRA, Everything the IRA wanted is in his statement," Paisley said.

Major's statement said Sinn Fein could hold talks at ministerial level with the British and Irish governments, which currently refuse any such meetings, if the IRA said it was giving up violence for good.
It could then publicly adopt a set of principles, drafted by Mitchell, committing the nationalists to non-violence and respect for democratic norms and the result of any negotiations.

The Irish government has voiced concern that a new IRA truce would not grant Sinn Fein automatic entry to the talks and the issue is expected to be the main agenda item when Irish Prime Minister John Bruton holds talks with Major in London on December 9.
